Acne (adult & adolescent)

Acne is a chronic inflammatory condition of the hair follicles and sebaceous glands. It's caused by a combination of hormonal stimulation of oil production, abnormal shedding of skin cells inside the follicle, the bacterium Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. Despite what's sometimes said, acne is not caused by poor hygiene — and over-washing usually makes it worse.

Common symptoms

  • Whiteheads and blackheads (comedones)
  • Inflamed red papules and pustules
  • Deeper nodules or cysts, often painful
  • Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark spots) or scarring
  • Adult-onset acne often appears along the jawline and lower face

When to seek care

If over-the-counter products haven't helped after 8–12 weeks, if you have cystic or nodular acne, if you're scarring, or if acne is significantly affecting how you feel about going to school, work, or in front of a camera — those are all reasonable times to see a dermatologist. Adult women with new-onset or jawline acne should also be evaluated.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Topical prescriptions: tretinoin, adapalene, clindamycin, azelaic acid, dapsone
  • Oral antibiotics for moderate inflammatory acne (typically time-limited)
  • Hormonal management for adult women (spironolactone, certain oral contraceptives)
  • Isotretinoin (Accutane) for severe nodulocystic or scarring acne — with iPLEDGE monitoring
  • In-office extractions and chemical peels for stubborn comedones and post-inflammatory marks

Expected timeline

Acne treatments work slowly. Topical retinoids take 8–12 weeks to show benefit. Oral antibiotics show meaningful change at 6–8 weeks. Isotretinoin courses typically run 5–7 months. We schedule follow-ups accordingly — usually a 6-week check after starting a new regimen.

Eczema / Atopic Dermatitis

Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition characterized by an impaired skin barrier and an overactive immune response in the skin. It tends to run in families along with asthma and seasonal allergies (the "atopic march"), though it can begin at any age. The Pacific Northwest's dry indoor winter heat and damp outdoor mold tends to make eczema flare in characteristic patterns through the year.

Common symptoms

  • Intensely itchy, dry, or scaly patches — often on the inner elbows, behind the knees, neck, wrists, and ankles
  • Red, weepy, or crusted areas during flares
  • Thickened, leathery skin in chronically scratched areas (lichenification)
  • Sleep disruption from nighttime itching is extremely common, especially in children

When to seek care

If the rash is interfering with sleep, if you're using over-the-counter hydrocortisone almost daily, if there are signs of infection (oozing, golden crust, fever), or if a child's eczema is severe enough that the family is losing significant sleep over it — see us. Modern treatments have changed dramatically in the last few years.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Skin barrier rehabilitation: bathing technique, emollients, soak-and-seal protocols
  • Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, pimecrolimus), and PDE4 inhibitors (crisaborole, roflumilast)
  • Topical JAK inhibitors (ruxolitinib) for limited areas in select patients
  • Narrowband UVB phototherapy for widespread disease
  • Systemic biologics for moderate-to-severe disease: dupilumab, tralokinumab, lebrikizumab, oral JAK inhibitors
  • Wet-wrap therapy training for severe pediatric flares

Expected timeline

Acute flares typically calm within 1–2 weeks of appropriate treatment. Establishing a sustainable maintenance routine — the part that actually keeps eczema controlled long-term — usually takes 2–3 visits over 2–3 months.

Psoriasis

Psoriasis is an immune-mediated condition in which skin cells turn over much faster than normal, producing well-defined, thickened red plaques covered with silvery scale. It's a systemic disease — meaning what you see on the skin is connected to inflammation that can also affect the joints (psoriatic arthritis), cardiovascular system, and metabolic health. Modern understanding has shifted significantly away from treating psoriasis as just a skin condition.

Common symptoms

  • Thick, red plaques with silvery-white scale, often on elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back
  • Itching or burning, though psoriasis is often less itchy than eczema
  • Nail pitting, lifting, or thickening
  • Scalp involvement that can extend to the hairline and behind the ears
  • Joint pain or stiffness, particularly morning stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes — may indicate psoriatic arthritis

When to seek care

Any new plaques or worsening psoriasis warrants evaluation, especially with new joint symptoms. If you have psoriasis covering more than a few patches of skin, modern systemic therapy may be a substantially better fit than continued topicals alone.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, and combination products
  • Narrowband UVB phototherapy (in-office or home unit)
  • Systemic non-biologic therapy (methotrexate, apremilast, deucravacitinib)
  • Biologic therapy targeting IL-17, IL-23, or TNF-alpha pathways — including ixekizumab, guselkumab, risankizumab, adalimumab
  • Coordination with rheumatology for psoriatic arthritis

Expected timeline

Topical regimens show response in 2–4 weeks. Biologics show meaningful clearing in 12–16 weeks and often produce dramatic improvement. Maintenance is ongoing.

Rosacea

Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition of the facial skin characterized by persistent redness, visible blood vessels, and sometimes acne-like bumps. It often begins between ages 30 and 50, more commonly in fair-skinned people, but occurs in all skin types. The mechanism involves abnormal vascular reactivity, neurogenic inflammation, and an altered skin microbiome.

Common symptoms

  • Persistent flushing across cheeks, nose, chin, and forehead
  • Visible small blood vessels (telangiectasias)
  • Inflammatory papules and pustules without blackheads (distinguishing it from acne)
  • Ocular involvement — gritty, burning, or red eyes (ocular rosacea, often missed)
  • Thickening of the nose (phymatous rosacea, more common in older men)

When to seek care

If your face is regularly red, if certain foods or temperature changes trigger predictable flushing, or if you have eye symptoms along with facial redness, an evaluation is worthwhile. Rosacea progresses if untreated.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Trigger identification (heat, alcohol, spicy foods, sun, stress are common)
  • Topical metronidazole, ivermectin, azelaic acid, and brimonidine
  • Oral doxycycline at sub-antimicrobial doses for inflammatory papules
  • IPL (intense pulsed light) and pulsed-dye laser for persistent redness and visible vessels
  • Referral to ophthalmology for ocular rosacea

Expected timeline

Inflammatory bumps respond in 6–8 weeks. Persistent redness and visible vessels typically require laser/IPL — 3 sessions spaced a month apart is a common starting course.

Skin Cancer Screening (annual skin exam)

A total-body skin examination is a head-to-toe visual evaluation of your skin, scalp, nails, and mucous membranes for moles, growths, or lesions that could be skin cancer or precancers. We use a dermatoscope — a handheld magnifying device with polarized light — to look more closely at anything concerning.

Who should be screened

  • Personal history of skin cancer, including basal cell, squamous cell, or melanoma
  • Family history of melanoma
  • Many moles (more than 50), or any atypical moles
  • Fair skin, blonde or red hair, blue or green eyes — particularly with a history of significant sun exposure or sunburns
  • Immunosuppression, including organ transplant recipients
  • Tanning bed use, particularly before age 35

What to expect at the visit

You'll change into a gown for a thorough exam. We examine the scalp, ears, face, neck, chest, abdomen, back, arms, legs, hands, feet, and (with your permission) the groin and buttock area, since melanomas occur in sun-protected areas too. The exam itself takes 10–15 minutes. Any concerning lesions are photographed for tracking or biopsied at the same visit.

Frequency

For average-risk adults, screening intervals are individualized based on findings. Higher-risk patients (prior melanoma, atypical mole syndrome, transplant recipients) are typically seen every 3–6 months.

Melanoma

Melanoma is a cancer that arises from melanocytes — the pigment-producing cells of the skin. It is far less common than basal or squamous cell carcinoma, but more dangerous because of its potential to spread. When caught early, melanoma is almost always curable with surgery alone. The single most important variable in melanoma outcome is depth at the time of diagnosis.

What to watch for — the ABCDEs

  • Asymmetry — one half doesn't match the other
  • Border — irregular, scalloped, or poorly defined
  • Color — varied within the lesion, including black, brown, tan, red, white, or blue
  • Diameter — larger than 6mm (about the size of a pencil eraser), though melanomas can be smaller
  • Evolving — changing in size, shape, color, or symptoms over weeks to months

The "ugly duckling" sign — a mole that looks different from your other moles — is also a useful clue.

When to seek care

Any new, changing, or unusual mole should be evaluated. Don't wait. If something doesn't look or feel right, it's reasonable to come in even between annual skin checks.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Biopsy for histologic diagnosis (we read all of our pathology through our OHSU dermatopathology partnership)
  • Wide local excision for confirmed melanoma based on depth-appropriate margins
  • Mohs micrographic surgery for select melanoma in situ on cosmetically sensitive areas
  • Referral to surgical oncology and medical oncology for sentinel lymph node biopsy and systemic therapy for deeper or advanced disease
  • Ongoing high-risk surveillance after treatment
Basal Cell Carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in humans. It arises from the basal cells of the epidermis, typically in sun-exposed areas — the face, ears, scalp, neck, and back of the hands. It grows slowly and almost never spreads to distant sites, but it can cause significant local tissue destruction if neglected. It is, however, eminently treatable when addressed early.

Common appearances

  • A pearly, pink, or skin-colored bump with visible small blood vessels
  • A non-healing sore that bleeds, crusts, and heals, then opens again
  • A flat, scar-like white or yellow patch
  • A scaly red patch — particularly the superficial variant on the trunk

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Electrodessication and curettage (ED&C) for low-risk lesions in non-cosmetically-sensitive areas
  • Standard surgical excision with margins
  • Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk lesions, recurrent lesions, and lesions on the face, ears, hands, feet, and genitals
  • Topical therapies (imiquimod, 5-fluorouracil) for select superficial lesions
  • Referral for advanced therapy in the rare locally advanced or metastatic case

Expected outcome

Cure rates for primary basal cell carcinoma treated with Mohs surgery exceed 98% at five years. After treatment, you're at higher risk for additional skin cancers, so ongoing surveillance is important.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma

Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common skin cancer. It develops from the keratinocytes in the upper layers of the epidermis, usually in chronically sun-damaged skin. Unlike basal cell carcinoma, it has a small but real potential to spread, particularly in larger lesions, lesions on the lip or ear, lesions in immunosuppressed patients, and lesions with certain microscopic features.

Common appearances

  • A rough, scaly red patch (often arising from a precancerous actinic keratosis)
  • A firm, tender nodule that may have a central crust or ulceration
  • A non-healing sore
  • A new growth at the site of a scar, burn, or chronic wound

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Standard surgical excision for most cases
  • Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk SCC and lesions on the face, ears, hands, feet, and genitals
  • ED&C for very small, low-risk lesions in non-critical areas
  • Topical or photodynamic therapy for actinic keratoses (the precancerous precursor)
  • Coordination with surgical and medical oncology for advanced disease
Mole Evaluation

Most adults have 10–40 moles. The vast majority are completely benign and stay that way for life. But because melanoma can arise either from existing moles or as a new lesion, knowing how to evaluate a mole — and when to have one looked at — is one of the most useful skills in skin self-care.

What's normal

  • Most moles develop in the first 30 years of life and stabilize
  • Moles can darken slightly with sun exposure and pregnancy
  • Moles may slowly raise up and lose pigment over decades — this is usually a benign aging change

What's not normal

  • A new mole appearing in adulthood
  • A mole that itches, bleeds, or doesn't heal
  • A mole that looks different from your other moles (the "ugly duckling")
  • Any change in size, shape, or color over weeks to months

How we evaluate

We use a dermatoscope to look at moles in detail — the patterns visible under polarized light help distinguish benign from concerning lesions. When we're not sure, we either monitor with comparison photography or biopsy. There is no shame in biopsying something that turns out to be benign — that's the system working correctly.

Hair Loss

Hair loss has many causes, and the right treatment depends entirely on identifying the right diagnosis. The most common patterns we see are androgenetic alopecia (the genetic, hormonally-mediated thinning that affects both men and women), telogen effluvium (a synchronous shedding after illness, stress, postpartum, or weight loss), and alopecia areata (an autoimmune patchy hair loss).

What to expect at evaluation

  • Detailed history — onset, pattern, family history, medications, recent illnesses, diet
  • Scalp examination with magnification (trichoscopy)
  • Pull test to assess active shedding
  • Selective lab work (iron studies, thyroid, vitamin D, hormonal panels when indicated)
  • Scalp biopsy for scarring or atypical hair loss patterns

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Topical minoxidil and oral low-dose minoxidil for androgenetic alopecia
  • Finasteride or dutasteride for male and select female pattern hair loss
  • Spironolactone for female pattern hair loss with hormonal contribution
  • Intralesional corticosteroid injections for alopecia areata
  • JAK inhibitors for severe alopecia areata
  • Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) discussions for select patients

Realistic expectations

Hair loss treatments work slowly. Six months is the minimum window to evaluate response. The single most important thing in androgenetic alopecia is starting early — preserving hair is easier than regrowing it.

Hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating)

Primary focal hyperhidrosis is excessive sweating beyond what's needed for thermoregulation, typically affecting the underarms, palms, soles, or face. It's not a hygiene issue or a sign of anxiety — it's a neurologic miscommunication with the sweat glands, and it's eminently treatable.

Common impacts

  • Visible sweat through clothing
  • Difficulty gripping objects, paper, or tools
  • Skin maceration or recurrent fungal infections
  • Social and occupational avoidance

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Prescription-strength aluminum chloride antiperspirants
  • Topical glycopyrronium (Qbrexza) wipes
  • Oral anticholinergics for generalized sweating
  • Botulinum toxin (Botox) injections — typically lasting 4–6 months per treatment, often covered by insurance for axillary hyperhidrosis when conservative therapy has failed
  • Iontophoresis referral for palmar/plantar disease
Vitiligo

Vitiligo is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks melanocytes, the pigment-producing cells of the skin. The result is well-defined patches of white skin, often symmetric. It is not contagious, not painful, and does not directly affect physical health — but the psychological and social impact can be significant. Treatment has improved considerably in the last few years.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors
  • Topical ruxolitinib (Opzelura) — an approved JAK inhibitor cream for non-segmental vitiligo
  • Narrowband UVB phototherapy, often combined with topical therapy
  • Excimer laser for localized disease
  • Camouflage and sunscreen counseling
  • Mental health referral when desired — vitiligo can carry significant emotional weight

Expected timeline

Repigmentation is slow. Facial vitiligo responds best; hands and feet respond least. A reasonable initial trial is 6 months, often longer.

Warts & Molluscum Contagiosum

Common warts are benign growths caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infecting the upper layers of the skin. Molluscum contagiosum is a related, common viral skin infection particularly in children — small pearly bumps with a central dimple. Both are benign and most cases resolve eventually, but treatment is reasonable when lesions are bothersome, spreading, or in conspicuous locations.

Treatment options at Westgate

  • Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen freezing)
  • Topical salicylic acid protocols
  • Cantharidin application in-office (especially for molluscum and warts in children)
  • Topical immunotherapy (squaric acid) for resistant cases
  • Topical retinoids, imiquimod, or 5-fluorouracil for selected cases
  • Surgical curettage for resistant solitary lesions

Realistic expectations

Warts and molluscum often require multiple treatment sessions over weeks to months. Recurrence is common. Many resolve on their own within 1–2 years even without treatment, especially in children.

Pediatric Dermatology

Children's skin develops differently from adult skin, and many of the conditions that bring kids to a dermatologist are specific to childhood — or behave differently than they would in an adult. We see patients from infancy through adolescence, and try to make visits friendly enough that we get the cooperation we need to do a careful exam.

Common pediatric conditions we treat

  • Infantile and childhood atopic dermatitis
  • Diaper dermatitis and other infant rashes
  • Birthmark evaluation — café-au-lait spots, hemangiomas, port-wine stains, congenital nevi
  • Molluscum contagiosum and warts
  • Tinea (ringworm), impetigo, and other common pediatric infections
  • Adolescent acne
  • Hair pulling (trichotillomania), alopecia areata
  • Psoriasis (less common in childhood but does occur)

Our approach

We schedule pediatric visits with a little extra time. Children sit on the exam table with a parent if they want, the room temperature is kept comfortable, and we explain what we're doing in age-appropriate language before we do it. For procedures, we use topical numbing when possible and never minimize a kid's worry about a shot.

Cosmetic Concerns (overview)

Cosmetic dermatology addresses concerns about how the skin looks rather than how it functions medically. These services are elective and almost always not covered by insurance. We offer them because — done thoughtfully — they're a legitimate part of dermatologic care, and because we'd rather our patients have access to good information and good technique from people who already know their skin.

Areas we can help with

  • Fine lines, dynamic wrinkles, volume loss (Botox, fillers)
  • Sun damage, brown spots, melasma (chemical peels, lasers, prescription topicals)
  • Acne scarring (microneedling, fractional laser, subcision)
  • Visible blood vessels and persistent redness (IPL, pulsed-dye laser)
  • Unwanted hair (laser hair reduction discussions and referrals)
  • Scar revision after surgery or injury

How we approach cosmetic visits

Cosmetic consultations are scheduled as separate visits from medical dermatology and are billed separately. We will tell you honestly if we don't think a procedure will accomplish what you're hoping for, or if a different approach would serve you better. We don't sell packages or run high-pressure consultations.
